narrative.text: Introduces the French edition, explaining that it draws on the UNFPA/WHO consultation held in Montreux in March 2006 and aims to alert stakeholders in sexual and reproductive health, immunization, child and adolescent health and cancer control to key issues in preparing for HPV vaccines.

Describes cervical cancer as the second most common cancer in women, with about 500 000 new cases and 250 000 deaths yearly, mostly in low-income countries, and nearly all linked to HPV. It explains the natural history of HPV infection, the role of screening in prevention and the potential of visual inspection with acetic acid and cryotherapy in low-resource settings. It also refers to the 2005 World Health Assembly resolution on cancer control and notes that early invasive cancer can be cured by surgery or radiotherapy.

Explains that HPV vaccines consist of non-infectious virus-like particles and that two prophylactic vaccines were highly effective against persistent infection and cervical lesions. It notes that questions remain on long-term efficacy, need for boosters and use in pregnant women and immunocompromised people.

Explains that HPV vaccination should ideally occur before sexual debut, since infection is acquired soon after, and describes the likely licensed age range and expected availability of the two vaccines. It discusses uncertain benefits for males, younger children, people with HIV and pregnant women. It links vaccine introduction to WHO's reproductive health strategy, which calls for using existing services as entry points.
Notes that HPV vaccines could strengthen links between health services and prevent a common cancer and widespread genital dysplasia and warts on a large scale, and introduces their main features.

Explains that HPV vaccines require new delivery approaches, target a different population from usual immunization programmes and involve multiple stakeholders in the sensitive field of sexual health. It describes the Global Immunization Vision and Strategy's plan to extend immunization beyond infants and the priority choices facing cancer control programmes. It presents the vaccines as a chance to encourage delayed sexual debut and condom use through strong partnerships.

Notes that HPV vaccines will likely cost much more than traditional EPI vaccines, with international financing such as GAVI under discussion. It warns that private-sector introduction among wealthier groups could deepen health inequalities unless strong public-private partnerships are built.

Stresses that HPV vaccine delivery must reflect each country's costs, feasibility and cultural acceptability, as vaccinating young girls against a sexually transmitted infection may be sensitive. It calls for avoiding backlash, giving complementary prevention messages and using the vaccine to build synergy between immunization, cancer control and sexual health programmes.

Argues that the vaccines' special features require new ways for programmes to work together and with the private sector, and international partnerships to speed access in developing countries. It highlights the need for balanced communication on the vaccines' benefits and limits within a broad cervical cancer prevention strategy.

Sets out key messages for presenting HPV vaccines, including that HPV causes over 99% of cervical cancers, is very common and highly contagious, and often goes unnoticed. It stresses explaining clearly what the vaccine can and cannot do, alongside lifestyle information given to young people.

Lists action points on advocacy, information and communication, such as gathering national data on cancer burden, HPV strains and age of sexual debut, and tailoring communication to decision-makers, health workers, women and communities. It also covers materials, training and financing questions such as insurance coverage. It urges using HPV vaccination to strengthen existing programmes for adolescents, including school-based sexual health, nutrition, tobacco and HIV education.

Discusses, in French, delivering HPV vaccination to target groups, noting that licensing will probably cover ages 9–26, split into a main group of girls aged 9–13, to be reached before sexual activity begins, and a catch-up group. It considers delivery through schools, adolescent services and other contact points and the challenges of each. It urges that HPV vaccination be offered within comprehensive, rights-based services rather than as a stand-alone strategy.

Advises, in French, that HPV vaccination programmes build on existing structures such as the vaccine cold chain to be cost-effective, and use partnerships with programmes and providers already in contact with target groups and women.

Explains, in French, the need to plan monitoring and evaluation of HPV vaccination from the outset, using routine immunization surveillance for process indicators. It notes that effects on genital warts and precancerous lesions will appear before effects on cancer, and that reporting of adverse events, including by the private sector, will be important.

Lists, in French, the actions national programmes should take on service delivery, such as linking the many actors involved, defining the main target group, tackling sociocultural barriers to vaccinating young adolescents, assessing school enrolment and setting process and outcome indicators.

Discusses, in French, overall management and financing of HPV vaccination, calling for resources from international sources and national health budgets within a broad strategy to strengthen health systems. It covers the high cost of the vaccines, the need for affordable prices and international funding commitments. It also addresses regulatory tasks after licensing, such as private-sector adverse event reporting, post-marketing surveillance and package inserts.

Lists, in French, the management and financing actions needed, starting with a national working group to coordinate health programmes, civil society and the private sector in drafting an HPV vaccination strategy. It also calls for more information on some issues and for full guidelines and protocols on giving the vaccines.

Concludes, in French, that HPV vaccination meets an important public health need as part of comprehensive cervical cancer control, that universal access to prevention, screening and treatment is crucial and that equity questions must be addressed. It ends with a note on the conditions for which the quadrivalent vaccine was licensed by the US FDA.
Lists, in French, further sources of information, with websites of UNFPA, WHO, the Global Immunization Vision and Strategy and the GAVI Alliance, and the WHO departments to contact.

The front matter of the French edition of WHO's 2006 guidance on preparing for the introduction of HPV vaccines (WHO/RHR/06.11), with copyright, disclaimers and contents. It notes that the content stems from a March 2006 technical consultation of experts on sexual and reproductive health programmes and HPV vaccines. It lists the participating experts and the UNFPA and WHO departments involved.
